title: A Black Drop on the Sun: The Transits of Venus
subtitle: The first world-wide scientific collaboration: 6 June 1761 and 3–4 June 1769, from Siberia to Tahiti
intro: On 6 June 1761 and again on 3–4 June 1769, Venus passed across the face of the sun, a pair of events that would not come again until 1874 and 1882. Edmond Halley had shown in 1716 that if observers far apart on the Earth timed the planet's entry and exit, the small differences in their times would give the distance to the sun, the unit by which the whole solar system is measured. To do it, astronomers had to be at the ends of the Earth at the same hour, with good clocks, known positions and clear skies.

What followed was the first planned world-wide scientific collaboration. In 1761, despite the Seven Years' War, about 120 observers at some 60 sites took part; in 1769, about 150 observations came from 77 stations, from Hudson Bay to Tahiti and from Vardø to Baja California. The convergence days in this chapter are the transit days themselves: on each, eight or more of these eyes are looking at the same small black disc from places thousands of kilometres apart.

The honest record is mostly not private diaries. It is observing logs and published reports, letters dated to establish what was sent when, travel journals written up afterwards (Chappe, Le Gentil), and a few true diaries (Sajnovics at Vardø, Wales's weather journal at Churchill, Cook's ship's journal). The form tags say which is which. Some eyes appear through letters about their work rather than their own words, and the Russian stations are thinly documented here.

Laid side by side, the entries show the race in an odd form. It was not a race between rivals for one discovery, but a race against weather, war, epidemic and the post. Chappe saw both transits and died of the second; Le Gentil waited eight years and saw neither; Mason and Dixon nearly turned back after a sea battle; Hell's late report led to an accusation of fraud that took a century to clear. One observer, Lomonosov, saw something no one asked him to look for and claimed an atmosphere around Venus, a claim still argued over.

The claims ledger follows the numbers. The 1761 results gave values for the solar parallax (the angle that fixes the sun's distance) ranging from about 8.3 to over 10 seconds of arc. The 1769 reductions published between 1770 and 1774, by William Smith, Hornsby, Lalande, Pingré, Lexell, Planman and Hell, narrowed it to 8.43–8.80 seconds. Encke's re-reduction of 1824 gave 8.58 seconds, and the modern value is about 8.794. The ledger reports these as each computer's claims, not as a verdict.
calendar_note: All date_iso values are Gregorian. Britain had used the Gregorian calendar since 1752, as had France, Spain and the Habsburg lands; Russia still used the Julian calendar, eleven days behind, so Russian dates (Lomonosov, Rumovsky, Chappe in Russia) show the Old Style date in date_display. Times are local apparent or mean time at the observing station, as the observers recorded them. The 1769 transit straddled the date line: it fell on 3 June for observers in the Americas, the Pacific and Europe, but on the morning of 4 June in India, which is why Le Gentil's entry carries that date. Cook's journal uses the nautical day, but its transit date matches the civil one.

eyes.name: Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche
eyes.role: Abbé and astronomer of the Académie royale des sciences, aged 33 in 1761 and 41 in 1769
eyes.side: France (Académie royale des sciences), hosted by Russia in 1761 and by Spain in 1769
eyes.where: Tobolsk, Siberia (1761); mission of San José del Cabo, Baja California (1769)
eyes.vantage_label: expedition observer at the telescope, twice
eyes.authenticity: Voyage en Sibérie (Paris, 1768) is his own edited account of the 1761 journey; a heavily abridged English version appeared in 1770. Voyage en Californie (Paris, 1772) was assembled after his death by César-François Cassini de Thury from his papers, which the engineer Pauly carried home. The California account mixes Chappe's own notes with Pauly's narrative of the epidemic.
eyes.bio: The only astronomer to reach his station for both transits and to see both. In 1761 he raced by sledge across Russia and timed the whole transit at Tobolsk under Cossack guard; in 1769 he crossed to New Spain, made one of the best observations anywhere, and died of the epidemic he had refused to flee. His two journeys show the expeditions' real cost.

sources.title: Linda Hall Library, Scientist of the Day: Jean-Baptiste Chappe d'Auteroche
Chappe, Voyage en Californie (1772), scan on the IMCCE Venus-transit history CD
Spanish edition with introduction by Marco A. Moreno Corral (UNAM, 2010)
American Scientist, Transits, Travels and Tribulations III and IV

eyes.name: Guillaume Le Gentil de la Galaisière
eyes.role: Astronomer of the Académie royale des sciences, aged 35 when he sailed
eyes.where: At sea in the Indian Ocean (1761); Pondicherry, India (1769)
eyes.vantage_label: expedition observer who saw nothing useful, twice
eyes.authenticity: Voyage dans les mers de l'Inde, two volumes, Paris 1779 and 1781, written up from his journals after his return. It is a later, shaped account, not day-by-day entries.
eyes.bio: Le Gentil left France in 1760 and did not return for eleven years. War kept him off his station in 1761, so he stayed in the Indian Ocean for the next transit, surveyed Madagascar, tried Manila, settled on Pondicherry, and was clouded out on the one morning that mattered. He came home to find himself declared dead, his seat taken and his estate divided.

sources.title: Le Gentil, Voyage dans les mers de l'Inde (1779), vol. 1, IMCCE scan
Le Gentil, Voyage dans les mers de l'Inde, vol. 2, IMCCE scan
Wikipedia: Guillaume Le Gentil

eyes.name: Charles Mason
eyes.role: Assistant at the Royal Observatory, Greenwich, aged 32; sent with the surveyor Jeremiah Dixon (1733–1779)
eyes.where: HMS Seahorse in the Channel; then the Cape of Good Hope
eyes.authenticity: His letters of 12 and 25 January 1761 to Charles Morton, Secretary of the Royal Society, are in the Society's archive (MM/10). The Cape results were printed in Philosophical Transactions vol. 52 (1762). Mason's voyage journal is held at Pennsylvania State University.
eyes.bio: Mason and Dixon were bound for Bencoolen in Sumatra when a French frigate mauled their ship a day out. They begged to give up; the Society refused, and they ended up at the Cape, where they caught the end of the transit. The partnership led straight to their famous survey line in America.

sources.title: Royal Society archive: Mason to Morton, 12 January 1761
Royal Society archive: Mason and Dixon to Morton, 25 January 1761
Phil. Trans. 52 (1762) pp. 611–628, Cape observations (IMCCE scan)

eyes.name: Nevil Maskelyne
eyes.role: Clergyman-astronomer aged 28 in 1761; Astronomer Royal from 1765
eyes.where: St Helena (1761); Greenwich, as planner and collector of results (1769)
eyes.vantage_label: expedition observer (clouded out), later the organiser
eyes.authenticity: His St Helena work and the lunar-distance method are in Phil. Trans. and The British Mariner's Guide (1763). His 1768 printed instructions for observers and his letters to Franklin are documented in the Franklin Papers.
eyes.bio: Maskelyne's 1761 expedition failed to see the transit, but the voyage let him test the lunar-distance method of finding longitude. As Astronomer Royal he became the clearing-house for the British 1769 effort, writing the instructions observers carried and receiving their results.

sources.title: MacTutor biography of Nevil Maskelyne
Franklin to Winthrop, 2 July 1768 (notes on Maskelyne's instructions)

eyes.name: Alexandre-Guy Pingré
eyes.role: Canon of Sainte-Geneviève and astronomer, aged 49, with his assistant Denis Thuillier
eyes.where: Rodrigues Island, Indian Ocean (1761); Cap-François, Saint-Domingue (1769)
eyes.vantage_label: expedition observer, half clouded, then caught in a raid
eyes.authenticity: His Rodrigues journal survives as a long manuscript, including about a hundred pages on the British capture of the island; it was not printed in full in his lifetime. His later computations appeared in the Mémoires of the Académie.
eyes.bio: An elderly canon who sailed through a war zone, Pingré saw only a cloudy half-hour of the 1761 transit, then watched British warships take the island. He went on to choose stations for 1769 and to compute one of the most-cited parallax values from the combined results.

sources.title: Chasing Venus: Pingré in Rodrigues (local history blog summarising his journal)
Pingré 1767, Mémoire sur le choix des lieux… Vénus 1769 (IMCCE scan)

eyes.name: Mikhail Vasilyevich Lomonosov
eyes.role: Polymath of the St Petersburg Imperial Academy of Sciences, aged 49
eyes.where: The roof of his own house on the Moika, St Petersburg
eyes.vantage_label: home observer who saw something no one else made sense of
eyes.authenticity: Published as a pamphlet in July 1761 in 250 copies, with a German version distributed abroad. An English translation with commentary was posted by Shiltsev and colleagues (arXiv 1206.3489, 2012). Whether his small telescope could have shown the effect he described is debated (Pasachoff and Sheehan, 2012, against; reconstruction observers in 2012, for).
eyes.bio: Lomonosov watched with a small refractor from home and saw, as Venus left the sun, a bright bulge on the solar edge ahead of the planet. He read it as sunlight bending through an atmosphere around Venus, the claim that has made his rooftop the most argued-about station of 1761.

sources.title: Shiltsev et al., Lomonosov's Discovery of Venus Atmosphere in 1761: English translation with commentaries (arXiv)
Pasachoff & Sheehan, Lomonosov, the discovery of Venus's atmosphere, and eighteenth-century transits of Venus, JAHH 15 (2012)

eyes.name: Stepan Yakovlevich Rumovsky
eyes.role: Astronomer of the St Petersburg Academy, aged 26 in 1761; a former pupil of Euler
eyes.where: Selenginsk beyond Lake Baikal (1761); Kola on the Murman coast (1769)
eyes.authenticity: His 1761 results were printed as Brevis expositio observationum… (St Petersburg, 1762). Day-by-day details of both journeys were not reachable for this chapter; his entries here are deliberately thin.
eyes.bio: Rumovsky led Russia's own 1761 expedition into Siberia and in 1769 observed from Kola while helping coordinate the largest national network of that year, stretching from the Arctic to the Caspian and Yakutsk. He is the Russian Academy's working counterpart to the French stars.

sources.title: Rumovsky 1762, Brevis expositio (IMCCE scan)
ESO VT-2004 Extended Information Sheet F6 (observing sites)

eyes.name: Maximilian Hell
eyes.role: Jesuit, court astronomer in Vienna, aged 48 in 1769; invited by Christian VII of Denmark-Norway
eyes.where: Vienna (1761); the fortress island of Vardø, Finnmark (1769)
eyes.vantage_label: expedition observer, later accused of cooking his numbers
eyes.authenticity: His Vardø report was printed in Copenhagen in 1770. In 1835 Karl Ludwig Littrow published extracts of his manuscripts and accused him of altering them; Simon Newcomb re-examined the manuscripts and cleared him in 1883. His own Vardø diary materials and Sajnovics's diary survive in Vienna.
eyes.bio: Hell spent nearly nine months at Vardø, above the Arctic Circle, measuring aurora, tides, magnetism and weather while waiting for one night. He got his observation through breaks in the cloud, then took more than a year to publish, a delay that turned into a suspicion that shadowed him for a century.

sources.title: Hansen & Aspaas, Maximilian Hell's geomagnetic observations in Norway 1769 (Tromsø Geophysical Observatory Reports 2, 2005)
Aspaas & Kontler, Maximilian Hell (1720–92) and the Ends of Jesuit Science (open access, Austria-Forum)
Vatican Observatory: Maximilian Hell (2022)

eyes.name: János Sajnovics
eyes.vantage_label: assistant and diarist at the station
eyes.authenticity: His travel diary survives in manuscript (Vienna) and was used, partly published, by Littrow in 1835; it is a chatty travel account with brief notes on daily science and weather. His Demonstratio idioma Ungarorum et Lapponum idem esse was printed in Copenhagen in 1770.
eyes.bio: Sajnovics is the assistant whose diary gives the hour-by-hour weather of the Vardø transit day. While there he noticed that the Sámi language resembled his own Hungarian, and his 1770 Demonstratio became a founding text of Finno-Ugric linguistics: a second discovery that came out of an astronomy trip.

sources.title: Aspaas, Standing on the shoulders of Scandinavian giants? Nordlit 50 (2022)
Hansen & Aspaas (2005), on Sajnovics's diary

eyes.name: James Cook
eyes.role: Lieutenant RN, aged 40, commander of HM Bark Endeavour and appointed observer
eyes.vantage_label: commander and observer at the station
eyes.authenticity: Holograph journal in the National Library of Australia; printed by Wharton (1893) and Beaglehole (1955). Uses the nautical day; the transit date matches the civil date here.
eyes.bio: Cook was chosen to carry Green and the Royal Society's instruments to Tahiti, a sealed second order sending him on to look for a southern continent. His journal shows the transit as the mission's fixed point, and his sketch of the planet's smeared edge became a famous image of the black drop.

sources.title: South Seas transcript of Cook's journal, 3 June 1769
National Library of Australia: Transit of Venus

eyes.name: Charles Green
eyes.role: Former assistant at the Royal Observatory, aged 34, the Royal Society's astronomer on the Endeavour
eyes.authenticity: His and Cook's observations were printed in Phil. Trans. 61 (1771); his own log is fragmentary. He died before the results were published.
eyes.bio: A Greenwich assistant of humble background, Green was the professional astronomer of the Endeavour, teaching the officers lunar distances on the way. He timed the transit beside Cook and Solander and died of dysentery on the way home, so he never saw his numbers in print.

sources.title: Captain Cook Society: Charles Green, man without a face
Phil. Trans. 61 (1771) pp. 397–405 (IMCCE scan)

eyes.name: David Rittenhouse
eyes.role: Self-taught clock- and instrument-maker, aged 37, observing for the American Philosophical Society
eyes.side: British North America (Pennsylvania; American Philosophical Society)
eyes.where: His farm observatory at Norriton, Pennsylvania
eyes.vantage_label: colonial observer at his own station
eyes.form: published observations; dated letters about them
eyes.authenticity: The Norriton observations, with William Smith's account, were printed in Transactions of the American Philosophical Society vol. 1 (1771). The often-told story that Rittenhouse fainted at the crucial moment comes from later accounts, notably his nephew William Barton's memoir (1813); Cadwalader Evans's letter of 11 June 1769 says Rittenhouse saw the contact first.
eyes.bio: Rittenhouse built his own observatory and clock for the transit, and the colonial observers, at Norriton, Philadelphia and Cape Henlopen, became the first big scientific effort of the American Philosophical Society. The quarrel over who was named first in the papers shows that credit mattered as much there as in Paris.

sources.title: Cadwalader Evans to Benjamin Franklin, 11 June 1769 (Founders Online)
IMCCE: Venus 1769, Rittenhouse

eyes.name: William Wales
eyes.role: Mathematician and computer for the Nautical Almanac, aged about 34, sent with Joseph Dymond
eyes.side: Britain (Royal Society, with the Hudson's Bay Company)
eyes.where: Prince of Wales Fort, Churchill River, Hudson Bay
eyes.vantage_label: expedition observer who wintered for it
eyes.authenticity: Wales's journal of the voyage and wintering was printed in Phil. Trans. vol. 60 (1770). He says himself that from September 1768 to late August 1769 he kept no journal except of the weather, so his transit day survives in the observation report rather than in prose.
eyes.bio: Wales and Dymond spent a sub-Arctic winter at the Hudson's Bay Company fort to catch a few hours of transit. His journal of brandy freezing in the observatory is the coldest page of the whole enterprise. He later sailed as astronomer on Cook's second voyage.

sources.title: Captain Cook Society: William Wales's journal of his first voyage, part 3
Dictionary of Canadian Biography: Wales, William

eyes.name: Joaquín Velázquez Cárdenas de León
eyes.role: Mexican-born lawyer, mathematician and astronomer, aged 36, attached to Visitor-General José de Gálvez
eyes.where: A hill above the mining camp of Real de Santa Ana, south-west of La Paz, Baja California
eyes.vantage_label: American-born observer at his own station
eyes.authenticity: His observations were sent to Chappe and to Spanish officials on 4 June 1769 and were printed by Cassini in Voyage en Californie (1772), with a transcription error of about two minutes of arc in Santa Ana's position. English translation in Nunis (ed.), The 1769 Transit of Venus (Los Angeles, 1982).
eyes.bio: A creole scholar from New Spain, Velázquez set up his own station on a hill near Santa Ana, a day's ride from Chappe, and timed the transit independently. When the French and Spanish party was destroyed by epidemic, he carried on their work with their instruments. He is the non-European-born observer whose numbers sit in the French record.

sources.title: Moreno Corral, introduction to the Spanish edition of Chappe's Viaje a Baja California (UNAM, 2010)
Journal of San Diego History review of Nunis (ed.), The 1769 Transit of Venus
EcuRed: Joaquín Velázquez de León

eyes.name: Jérôme Lalande
eyes.role: Astronomer of the Académie royale des sciences, aged 29 in 1761
eyes.where: Palais du Luxembourg, Paris (1761); observatory of the Collège Mazarin, Paris (1769)
eyes.vantage_label: home observer and the clearing-house for results
eyes.authenticity: His observations and reductions appeared in the Histoire et Mémoires de l'Académie royale des sciences (1769 volume and after); manuscripts of 1771 are reproduced on the IMCCE CD.
eyes.bio: Lalande observed from Paris both times, but his real station was his desk: after Delisle he became the collector of the world's results, chasing late reports and turning them into a value for the sun's distance. His impatience with late senders helped feed the suspicion against Hell.

sources.title: IMCCE: Transit of Venus of 1769, observations made in Paris (Lalande)
Lalande 1771, manuscripts (IMCCE scan)

eyes.name: Benjamin Franklin
eyes.role: Colonial agent in London, Fellow of the Royal Society, aged 62
eyes.authenticity: Letters to and from Winthrop, Evans and Maskelyne are edited in The Papers of Benjamin Franklin and online at Founders Online, with editorial notes.
eyes.bio: Franklin did not observe either transit, but his letters show the network at work: chasing instrument-makers for colonial observers, urging an American station, and passing Pennsylvania's results to the Astronomer Royal amid local quarrels over credit.

sources.title: Franklin to John Winthrop, 2 July 1768
Franklin to Cadwalader Evans, 7 September 1769
John Winthrop to Franklin: On Observing the Transit of Venus, 6 September 1769

entries.headline: Le Gentil sails for India, fifteen months early
entries.digest: Le Gentil leaves France for Pondicherry, a French post on the Coromandel coast, with more than a year in hand. Britain and France are at war, and the timetable assumes the sea lanes stay open. By July he is at Isle de France (Mauritius), where the war stops him going further.
entries.source_note: Le Gentil, Voyage dans les mers de l'Inde (1779); Wikipedia and American Scientist summaries (sailed March 1760, Mauritius July 1760).

entries.headline: Chappe reaches Vienna on the long road to Siberia
entries.digest: Chappe left Paris in late November with instruments packed for a winter journey of thousands of kilometres. He reaches Vienna on the last day of the year, leaves on 8 January, and by late January is in Warsaw, about to cross Russia by sledge before the spring thaw makes the roads impassable.
entries.source_note: American Scientist, Transits, Travels and Tribulations III (itinerary dates).

entries.place: Portsmouth (dated); HMS Seahorse back in port
entries.headline: A French frigate wrecks the plan for Sumatra
entries.digest: Mason writes to the Royal Society's secretary that a 34-gun French frigate, L'Grand, attacked the Seahorse in the Channel, killing eleven men and wounding thirty-seven. The ship has had to turn back for repairs. Shaken, he tells the Society that the Sumatra station is now out of reach.
entries.source_note: Royal Society archive MM/10/128, catalogue description and quotation.

entries.headline: Maskelyne sails for St Helena
entries.digest: Maskelyne boards the East India ship Prince Henry for St Helena. He spends the voyage taking lunar distances with Tobias Mayer's tables, testing a way to find longitude at sea that will matter far beyond the transit.
entries.source_note: MacTutor biography of Maskelyne.

entries.headline: Mason and Dixon argue for a different station
entries.digest: Replying to two letters from the Society's secretary, Mason and Dixon say they cannot now reach any place east of the Cape soon enough to give a useful comparison with Greenwich and St Helena. They propose Scanderoon (Iskenderun) in the Levant instead. The Society insists they sail; they end up at the Cape itself.
entries.source_note: Royal Society archive MM/10/130, catalogue description.

entries.date_display: Tuesday 17 March 1761 (6 March O.S. in Russia)
entries.headline: Chappe leaves Moscow, racing the thaw
entries.digest: After St Petersburg, where the Academy has arranged his route, Chappe leaves Moscow eastward by sledge. Rivers are about to break up, and a wrecked sledge or a flooded crossing could cost him the transit. He reaches Tobolsk in mid-April and builds an observatory on a height above the town.
entries.source_note: American Scientist III (left Moscow 17 March, reached Tobolsk mid-April); Linda Hall Library.

entries.headline: Maskelyne lands with two months to spare
entries.digest: Maskelyne and his assistant Robert Waddington reach St Helena with time to choose a site and set up. The island was chosen as a southern station for comparison with Greenwich.
entries.source_note: MacTutor biography of Maskelyne.

entries.headline: A lunar eclipse fixes Tobolsk on the map
entries.digest: Chappe uses an eclipse of the moon to work out Tobolsk's longitude, without which his transit times would be useless for comparison. The spring floods have been severe, and some townspeople blame the foreign astronomer for interfering with the heavens; the governor provides a guard.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia, Chappe d'Auteroche (lunar eclipse of 18 May; floods; Cossack guard).

entries.headline: Pingré lands on Rodrigues nine days before
entries.digest: After an attack at sea in January and a forced stop at Isle de France, Pingré and Thuillier sight Rodrigues on 26 May and land on the 28th. They set up near the cove once used by the Huguenot castaway François Leguat.
entries.source_note: Rodrigues local-history summary of Pingré's journal (26 May sighted, 28 May landed).

entries.headline: British warships take the island
entries.digest: Soon after the transit, British ships capture Rodrigues, and the French ship meant to carry Pingré away is taken. His journal gives about a hundred pages to the capture and to his months as a stranded civilian, before he gets back to Isle de France.
entries.source_note: Rodrigues summary of Pingré's manuscript (capture described at length); exact dates not verified here.

entries.headline: Clear sky in Siberia: the whole transit timed
entries.digest: The day before was overcast, but on the morning of the transit the sky clears. Chappe times the planet's entry and exit and watches the whole passage, one of the few complete observations of 1761. He publishes the results first in St Petersburg; more than a century later they were still used in calculations of the sun's distance.
entries.source_note: Linda Hall Library; Wikipedia; American Scientist III.

entries.place: At sea, Indian Ocean, aboard a French frigate
entries.headline: Perfect weather, and a rolling deck
entries.digest: Le Gentil's ship, blown off course for weeks and then turned back when the captain learned that the British held Pondicherry, is still at sea on the day. The sky is clear and he sees Venus on the sun, but without a steady deck or a known position his times have no scientific value.
entries.source_note: Le Gentil, Voyage (1779); American Scientist III; Wikipedia.

entries.headline: At the Cape, only the planet's exit
entries.digest: The transit has already begun when the sun rises at the Cape, so Mason and Dixon can time only the end. Their egress times, sent to London, were among the useful southern results of 1761 and were reported to the Royal Society by James Short.
entries.source_note: IMCCE page on Mason (egress only); Short, Phil. Trans. 52 (1762) 611–628.

entries.headline: Clouds over St Helena
entries.digest: After months of preparation, the sky over St Helena is clouded and Maskelyne sees nothing useful. He stays on the island trying to measure the parallax of the star Sirius, until he concludes his instrument is faulty.
entries.source_note: MacTutor biography; IMCCE fiche 20b (bad weather at St Helena).

entries.headline: Half an hour of sun, and a strong wind
entries.digest: The weather is mostly bad. Between about eight and half past, local time, the clouds part, but a strong wind shakes the telescope and Pingré judges the observation far from satisfactory. He saves what he can for the computers in Paris.
entries.source_note: Rodrigues summary of Pingré's journal.

entries.place: His house on the Moika, St Petersburg
entries.headline: A bright rim around Venus
entries.digest: Watching through a small two-lens refractor with a lightly smoked glass, Lomonosov sees the sun's edge blur as Venus enters. As it leaves, a bright bulge forms on the solar edge ahead of the planet, grows and vanishes. He concludes that Venus has an atmosphere at least as large as Earth's, bending sunlight around its rim.
entries.source_note: Lomonosov's pamphlet in English translation with commentary, arXiv 1206.3489.

entries.headline: Russia's own expedition watches from beyond Baikal
entries.digest: Rumovsky observes at Selenginsk, with Nikita Popov at Irkutsk, the Russian Academy's answer to the French presence at Tobolsk. Their results are reduced in St Petersburg and published the next year.
entries.source_note: Lomonosov translation commentary (arXiv 1206.3489) lists Rumovsky at Selenginsk and Popov at Irkutsk; the weather and his exact results were not verified here.

entries.headline: Hell watches from Vienna
entries.digest: Hell, the Habsburg court astronomer, observes the transit from Vienna, where Cassini de Thury has also come to observe with the young Archduke Joseph. For Hell it is a home-station observation; eight years later he will travel to the edge of the Arctic for the next one.
entries.source_note: Vatican Observatory biography (observed 6 June 1761 in Vienna); IMCCE fiche 20b (Cassini at Vienna).

entries.headline: Lalande observes from the Luxembourg
entries.digest: Lalande watches from the Luxembourg palace in Paris, part of the home network against which the distant stations will be compared. Across Europe more than a hundred professional observers at about sixty sites are doing the same, many of them alerted by Delisle's map.
entries.source_note: IMCCE fiche 20b (Lalande at Luxembourg; Newcomb's count of 120 observers at 62 sites).

entries.headline: Lomonosov prints his atmosphere of Venus
entries.digest: Lomonosov's pamphlet on the appearance of Venus on the sun is printed in 250 copies, followed in August by a German version for foreign readers. It is the first published claim that Venus has an atmosphere, set out with sketches of what he saw at entry and exit.
entries.source_note: arXiv 1206.3489 (submitted 4 July, published 17 July 1761, O.S. as used by the Academy; date_iso converted).

entries.headline: Rumovsky publishes the Russian results
entries.digest: Rumovsky's Latin Brevis expositio presents the Russian observations of 1761 for the international community. Like the other first reductions, it shows how badly the scattered results agree: values for the sun's parallax from 1761 ran from about 8.3 to over 10 seconds of arc.
entries.source_note: IMCCE list of 1761 texts (Rumovsky 1762, Brevis Expositio); IMCCE fiche 20c (1761 spread).

entries.headline: Le Gentil settles in for the second chance
entries.digest: After mapping Madagascar's east coast and an unwelcoming stay at Spanish Manila, Le Gentil returns to Pondicherry, now French again under the 1763 peace. He builds a small observatory and has over a year to wait.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia (arrived Pondicherry March 1768, built observatory).

entries.headline: Chappe sails for New Spain
entries.digest: The Spanish crown has allowed a French expedition into its Pacific coast only with Spanish officers attached. Chappe leaves Cadiz with an engineer, an artist, a clockmaker and the naval officers Vicente de Doz and Salvador de Medina. The Atlantic crossing takes 77 days.
entries.source_note: American Scientist IV (sailed from Cadiz 8 March 1768, 77 days); IMCCE fiche 20c (party members).

entries.headline: Hell leaves Vienna for the Arctic
entries.digest: Invited by Christian VII of Denmark-Norway, Hell sets out with Sajnovics. They travel by way of Copenhagen and Christiania, spend three weeks in Trondheim and sail north along the coast, arriving at the fortress of Vardø on 11 October.
entries.source_note: Hansen & Aspaas (2005); Aspaas, Nordlit 50 (2022).

entries.headline: Franklin reports a run on instruments
entries.digest: Franklin tells John Winthrop at Harvard that the instrument-maker Bird is swamped: the Royal Society wants instruments for Siberia, the South Seas and Hudson's Bay, and France and Russia are ordering too. He passes on Maskelyne's wish for an astronomer at Lake Superior and urges Winthrop to go himself or send a pupil.
entries.source_note: Founders Online, Franklin to Winthrop, 2 July 1768, with editorial notes.

entries.headline: The Jesuits reach Vardø for the long wait
entries.digest: Hell and Sajnovics reach Vardø, a fortress island off the Arctic coast near the Russian border. They will spend nearly nine months there observing aurora, tides, magnetism and weather. Sajnovics's diary reads like a travel book, with only brief notes on the science.
entries.source_note: Hansen & Aspaas (2005); Nordlit 50 (2022).

entries.place: Prince of Wales Fort, Churchill River
entries.headline: Brandy freezes inside the observatory
entries.digest: The river is frozen across, and Wales records that a half-pint glass of English brandy has frozen solid inside the observatory. He and Dymond have been at the Hudson's Bay Company fort since August with seven months still to wait.
entries.source_note: Wales's journal, Phil. Trans. 60 (1770), via Captain Cook Society extract.

entries.headline: So cold the clock needs extra weight
entries.digest: In the depth of winter even the small alarm clock needs extra weight to keep running. Wales carries brandy outside and finds it thickened within minutes, and lies awake listening to the fort's beams crack in the frost.
entries.source_note: Wales's journal, Phil. Trans. 60 (1770), via Captain Cook Society extract.

entries.headline: A pig upsets the magnetic instrument
entries.digest: With the transit two weeks away, Sajnovics notes that a pig has knocked over the set-up for measuring magnetic dip. A comic entry, but a reminder that this station was a working farmyard at the edge of the world.
entries.source_note: Sajnovics's diary as summarised in Hansen & Aspaas (2005).

entries.place: San José del Cabo, Baja California
entries.headline: Landing into an epidemic with thirteen days left
entries.digest: After crossing Mexico and a slow voyage from San Blas, Chappe lands at the mission of San José del Cabo thirteen days before the transit. Local people warn of a terrible epidemic and advise him to go north, but there is no time to move the instruments. He sets up where he is.
entries.source_note: American Scientist IV (landed 13 days before the transit; epidemic warning). Day computed from that statement.

entries.headline: A cloudless day, and a blur no one expected
entries.digest: The day is perfectly clear, and Cook, Green and Solander follow the planet for about six hours from the fort. A dark haze clings to the planet's edge at the moments of contact, and their timings disagree by more than they should. Cook notes the heat was greater than anything they had yet felt.
entries.quote: not a Clowd was to be seen the Whole day
entries.source_note: Cook's journal, 3 June 1769 (South Seas transcript; NLA Transit of Venus page).

entries.headline: The astronomer times the contacts through the black drop
entries.digest: Green is the chief observer at the fort. As Venus enters, a dark band seems to tie the planet to the sun's edge, so the instant of contact cannot be fixed cleanly. Every station that day faced this black drop, which more than anything else limited the 1769 result.
entries.source_note: Green & Cook, Phil. Trans. 61 (1771) 397–421; Captain Cook Society biography of Green.

entries.headline: One of the best observations of the day
entries.digest: Under a clear sky Chappe records the planet's entry just before noon local time and its exit in the late afternoon, describing the black drop as he sees it. Sick colleagues and townspeople are already dying around the mission. His times turned out to be among the best of 1769.
entries.source_note: Moreno Corral's introduction (Chappe: ingress 11h 59m 17s, egress 5h 54m 50s); American Scientist IV; Wikipedia (black drop).

entries.place: Hill above Real de Santa Ana, Baja California
entries.headline: A Mexican observer times it on his own hill
entries.digest: Velázquez has climbed a hill near Santa Ana, because the town has no clear horizon. He records the first contact at 11h 55m 45s and the exit at 5h 53m 36s local time, an independent measurement a few dozen kilometres from Chappe's station.
entries.source_note: Moreno Corral's introduction to the 2010 Spanish edition of Chappe's Voyage.

entries.headline: Norriton sees the contact first
entries.digest: At the farm observatory Rittenhouse sees the contact first, then John Lukens, then William Smith, who signals and records. Rittenhouse's and Lukens's times nearly agree. A later family account says he fainted with the excitement; the contemporary letter about the observation does not mention it.
entries.source_note: Cadwalader Evans to Franklin, 11 June 1769 (Founders Online); fainting story from later accounts (Barton, 1813) flagged as such.

entries.place: Prince of Wales Fort, Hudson Bay
entries.headline: Cloud breaks at the right moments at Churchill
entries.digest: After the long winter, Wales and Dymond get good views of both the planet's entry and exit despite cloudy intervals. Their times go back to London on the company ship. The river ice does not break up until 16 June.
entries.source_note: American Scientist IV (good views at ingress and egress despite cloud; ice broke 16 June).

entries.date_display: Saturday 3 June 1769 (to the small hours of 4 June)
entries.headline: A day of clouds, then Venus after nine
entries.digest: Sajnovics records a grey morning, brief sun around three, more cloud brought by a south-west breeze, and cover until about eight in the evening. After nine the sun breaks through at intervals, three telescopes are trained on it and the entry is caught. A merchant fires nine guns and the fortress flag goes up.
entries.source_note: Sajnovics's diary as summarised in Aspaas & Kontler, Maximilian Hell (2020), p. 272 (Austria-Forum page 000286).

entries.headline: Under the midnight sun, Hell gets his contacts
entries.digest: With the sun never setting at Vardø, the transit runs from mid-evening into the small hours. Hell's party times the contacts through gaps in the cloud. The next day a solar eclipse saves the longitude measurement the winter's clouds had spoiled, without which the transit times could not be compared.
entries.source_note: Hansen & Aspaas (2005) (transit 3 June; eclipse of 4 June rescued the longitude); Aspaas & Kontler (2020).

entries.headline: Paris catches Venus at sunset
entries.digest: In Paris the transit begins only in the evening, so Lalande can see little before sunset at the Collège Mazarin. That hardly matters for his part. He is already collecting results that, by his count, will come from more than seventy stations.
entries.source_note: IMCCE page (Lalande observed at Collège Mazarin, 3 June 1769; Histoire de l'Académie 1769 pp. 417–425); 'little before sunset' follows from the transit timing and is not quoted from his memoir.

entries.headline: Russia's northern station at Kola
entries.digest: Rumovsky observes from Kola, one of a Russian network that stretches from Kola and Ponoi in the north to Guryev on the Caspian, Orsk, Orenburg and Yakutsk, with Euler's son, Lexell and Christian Mayer at St Petersburg. The empire is now an organiser of the enterprise, not just a host.
entries.source_note: ESO VT-2004 sheet F6 (sites and observers); Wikipedia (Rumovsky at Kola, coordinating). Weather and success at Kola not verified here.

entries.headline: Eight years of waiting, and a cloud
entries.digest: In India the transit falls on the morning of 4 June. The mornings of the previous weeks have all been fine, but on this one the sky is overcast and Le Gentil sees nothing. He later wrote that the loss almost drove him out of his mind.
entries.source_note: Le Gentil, Voyage (1779), as summarised by Wikipedia and Borders Sundials.

entries.headline: Velázquez sends his numbers to Chappe
entries.digest: The day after the transit, Velázquez sends a summary of his observations to Chappe in Latin and to the Spanish officials in Spanish. About 9 June Chappe replies that the figures are sound, a dated exchange that put the Mexican result on record next to the French one.
entries.source_note: Moreno Corral's introduction to the 2010 Spanish edition.

entries.headline: A quarrel over who saw it first
entries.digest: A week later Cadwalader Evans sends Franklin the Norriton, Philadelphia and Cape Henlopen observations and complains that the newspapers have listed William Smith before Rittenhouse, the far better mathematician. The colonial transit is already a fight over credit.
entries.source_note: Founders Online, Evans to Franklin, 11 June 1769.

entries.headline: A lunar eclipse, as the fever spreads
entries.digest: Chappe stays to observe an eclipse of the moon, needed to fix his longitude. The party is now falling sick one after another, and the plan to leave is put off as he nurses the sick.
entries.source_note: IMCCE fiche 20c (lunar eclipse of 18 June 1769); American Scientist IV.

entries.headline: Chappe dies at the mission
entries.digest: Chappe dies of the epidemic, probably typhus, and is buried at the mission of San José del Cabo; the engineer Pauly closes his eyes. Medina dies too, and most of the party. Pauly sends the papers in a casket to the viceroy and sets out for home.
entries.source_note: Moreno Corral introduction (death 1 August, buried at the mission); American Scientist IV (Pauly).

entries.headline: Franklin forwards Philadelphia to the Astronomer Royal
entries.digest: Franklin tells Evans he has passed the Pennsylvania observations straight to Maskelyne, who will compare them with all the others and report to the Royal Society. Other copies had gone to Thomas Penn instead, a sign of the colony's politics running through its science.
entries.source_note: Founders Online, Franklin to Evans, 7 September 1769.

entries.headline: Wales and Dymond are home
entries.digest: Wales and Dymond reach London after sailing from Churchill in early September. They are paid only once the Society judges the work well done; their results go into the British pool that Maskelyne and Hornsby will reduce.
entries.source_note: American Scientist IV.

entries.headline: Hell's report appears, late and long
entries.digest: Hell and Sajnovics stay in Copenhagen from October 1769 to May 1770, lecturing and editing. Hell's long, detailed report of the Vardø observations is printed under Danish royal auspices in 1770, well after other results had reached Paris, and the delay invites suspicion that he waited to see others' numbers.
entries.source_note: Vatican Observatory biography (published Copenhagen 1770); Aspaas & Kontler (2020) on lateness; Hansen & Aspaas (2005).

entries.place: Royal Danish Society of Sciences, Copenhagen
entries.headline: The assistant announces a different discovery
entries.digest: Sajnovics reads the first part of his paper arguing that Hungarian and Sámi are one language at root, built on words and grammar he collected in Finnmark. Two more sessions follow, and the first copy of the printed Demonstratio reaches him on 10 April.
entries.source_note: Aspaas, Nordlit 50 (2022).

entries.headline: Still waiting for the Russian numbers
entries.digest: Nine months after the transit, Lalande still has not received the Lowitz and Islenev observations from Guryev and Yakutsk. The world-wide experiment can only be finished at the speed of the slowest packet.
entries.source_note: Aspaas & Kontler (2020), footnote on Austria-Forum page 000293.

entries.headline: Cook records the death of Green
entries.digest: Among the many deaths from the dysentery and fever picked up at Batavia, Cook records that of the astronomer Charles Green. The transit times reach the Royal Society without the man who made them.
entries.source_note: Captain Cook Society biography of Green; Cook's journal, 29 January 1771.

entries.headline: Home after eleven years, declared dead
entries.digest: Delayed by dysentery and stranded by a storm at Île Bourbon, Le Gentil finally reaches Paris on a Spanish ship. He finds he has been declared legally dead, his seat in the Academy filled and his estate divided among relatives. It takes lawsuits and the king's intervention to restore him.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia; Borders Sundials.

convergences.label: First transit of Venus: 6 June 1761
convergences.note: The same few hours look completely different from each station. Chappe in Siberia gets a clear sky and the whole transit; Le Gentil sees it plainly from a rolling deck and can measure nothing; Maskelyne is clouded out; Pingré gets half an hour in a gale; Mason and Dixon at the Cape see only the end. In St Petersburg, Lomonosov, with no expedition at all, sees a glow on the planet's rim and comes away with a discovery rather than a measurement.

convergences.label: Second transit of Venus: 3–4 June 1769
convergences.note: The transit crosses the date line: noon in Baja California, morning in Tahiti, afternoon in Pennsylvania and Hudson Bay, evening at the Arctic's edge in Vardø and Kola, and the morning of 4 June in India. Tahiti, Baja and Pennsylvania have clear skies; Vardø and Churchill get through on cloud breaks; Le Gentil, who had waited longest, gets nothing. Almost everyone who does see it sees the same black drop, the blur that kept the result from the precision the planners had hoped for.

convergences.label: The morning after: data starts to move
convergences.note: Velázquez sends his times to Chappe; at Vardø a solar eclipse rescues Hell's longitude; in Pondicherry Le Gentil faces the fact of his loss. The experiment now becomes a postal one.

claims.claim: Mason reports the Seahorse battle and that the Sumatra station cannot be reached in time
Complete transit timed at Tobolsk, one of the few full observations of 1761
claims.evidence: Chappe's observing record; published St Petersburg, then Voyage en Sibérie (1768)

claims.claim: Bright bulge seen on the solar edge at egress; interpreted as refraction in an atmosphere of Venus

First printed claim that Venus has an atmosphere (Russian; German version August 1761). Contested: Pasachoff and Sheehan (2012) argue his telescope could not show it; Shiltsev and colleagues (2012) argue it could
Cape egress times printed in the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions, reported by James Short
Russian 1761 results published; values from 1761 overall range about 8.3" to 10.6"
Contact times at Tahiti, with the 'black drop' blurring the moment of contact
Independent times from Santa Ana: ingress 11h 55m 45s, egress 5h 53m 36s local
claims.evidence: Printed in Chappe, Voyage en Californie (1772); Moreno Corral (2010)

claims.claim: Sends his observation summary to Chappe (Latin) and Spanish officials; Chappe confirms about 9 June
William Smith's reduction of the Pennsylvania observations gives a solar parallax of 8.6045"
Vardø report printed in Copenhagen, after other results reached Paris; the delay prompts suspicion
Pauly, the sole French survivor, delivers Chappe's posthumous observations to the Académie
Lalande's combined solar parallax of 8.55" to 8.63" (others in 1770–72: Hornsby 8.78", Lexell 8.68", Planman 8.43")
Pingré's solar parallax of 8.80", at the top of the 1769 range of 8.43" to 8.80"
Hell's solar parallax of 8.70"; Encke's 1824 reduction of both transits later gives 8.5776"
claims.evidence: IMCCE fiche 20c; ESO VT-2004 sheet F5

claims.claim: Karl Ludwig Littrow publishes Hell's manuscripts and alleges altered figures; Simon Newcomb re-examines them and clears Hell in 1883

ties.note: Observed a short distance apart in Baja California, exchanged results by letter on 4 and about 9 June 1769; Velázquez later used the French instruments after Chappe's death.
Both observed 1761 under the St Petersburg Academy's umbrella: Chappe at Tobolsk by imperial invitation, Lomonosov at home. Lomonosov's commentary counts Chappe among the eight observers in Russia.
After the Cape, Mason and Dixon went on to St Helena, where Maskelyne was observing, before sailing home in convoy in early 1762.
Travelled and wintered together at Vardø; Sajnovics's diary is the day-by-day record of Hell's expedition and was later used against and for Hell in the forgery controversy.
Observed side by side at Fort Venus and published jointly in 1771; Cook recorded Green's death in January 1771.
After Hudson Bay, Wales sailed as astronomer on Cook's second voyage (1772–75), carrying the transit generation's methods into the Pacific.
Franklin received the Pennsylvania observations, including Rittenhouse's, and passed them to Maskelyne in September 1769.
Franklin relayed Maskelyne's call for an American station in 1768 and sent him the colonial results in 1769; Maskelyne wrote back in December 1769.
Lalande ran the Paris collection of results; Hell, organised from Copenhagen without consulting him, published late, and the resulting suspicion lasted until Newcomb cleared him in 1883.
Both reduced the combined 1769 results for the Académie, and their parallax values (8.80" and 8.55–8.63") bracket the French debate.
Both Académie astronomers sent to the Indian Ocean in 1761; both were caught by the British-French war at sea, one at Rodrigues and one off the Coromandel coast.
Mason and Dixon went on to survey the Pennsylvania–Maryland line (1763–68), and Rittenhouse was later one of the astronomers on the commissions that extended Pennsylvania's boundary west.

threads_out.note: The transit project rests on the telescope's first discoveries: Galileo's phases of Venus showed it orbits the sun, Kepler's tables predicted the 1631 transit, and Horrocks saw the 1639 one. Halley's 1716 plan to use transits to measure the sun's distance turned that line of work into a world-wide experiment.

The Endeavour's public purpose was the 1769 transit: Cook and Green's observations at Fort Venus are the Tahiti station of this chapter, and the sealed second order that sent the ship on to New Zealand and Australia was opened only after it.

Humboldt, surveying New Spain in 1803–04, worked with the astronomical positions left by Velázquez de León and his colleagues, the same Mexican tradition of measurement that put its own times beside Chappe's in 1769.

Six years before the first transit, the same correspondence networks, the Royal Society's Philosophical Transactions and the Paris Académie, gathered eyewitness reports of the Lisbon earthquake and sea wave from across Europe: practice for the collect-and-compare science of 1761.

The epidemic, probably typhus, that killed Chappe and most of his party at San José del Cabo in 1769, and the Batavia fevers that killed Green in 1771, belong to the Long Threads chapter's story of disease moving along routes of empire and trade.
